opus-5.5.text:
Well, let me start by saying I think AI is an extraordinary technology. It's going to raise productivity enormously, and in the long run it could be one of the greatest things that's ever happened to us. So the problem isn't the technology. The problem is the dynamic around it, and I look at that the way I look at any machine: how does the cause-and-effect relationship work?

What happens in every great technological boom is that people get excited, and rightly so. The technology is real, just as railroads, electricity and the internet were real. But the excitement draws in enormous amounts of capital, and prices start to discount a future that may be wonderful but can't justify what's being paid for it. Then you start to finance it with debt. Now you have promises to deliver money, and you have to be able to produce the cash flows to service those promises. That's the classic bubble dynamic. You can be right about the technology and still lose a lot of money, because the question isn't whether it's a great technology. The question is whether the revenues will be there, in time, to pay for it all. And when you need to sell assets or borrow to meet those obligations, that's when the thing can break.

The second problem is who benefits. A relatively small number of companies, and the people who own them, are getting a very large share of the gains. Meanwhile, you already have enormous wealth and values gaps, and now you have a technology that can replace a lot of people's work. The top maybe 10 percent gets more productive and richer, and a large part of the population doesn't get much of that benefit and may lose out. When you have large wealth gaps and bad financial conditions at the same time, you get conflict. History shows that very clearly, and that's when you see populism of the left and the right, and internal fights over who gets what.

The third problem is geopolitical. Whoever wins the technology war tends to win the economic war and the military war. So the United States and China can't really afford to slow down, and neither can the companies, because each fears what happens if the other gets there first. Everybody is compelled to invest, even when it may not make financial sense.

So when you put those together, you have debt, internal conflict over wealth, and great power conflict, all being amplified by this technology. Those are the forces I've studied throughout history, and they're interacting now. That doesn't mean AI is bad. It means that if we don't handle it well, the same thing that creates this incredible productivity can also create a financial bust and a lot of social and political disorder. The question is whether we can be smart enough to manage it, and to spread the benefits so that it works for most people.

r001.rationale: The response says companies are compelled to invest because they fear a rival will get there first, even when the investment may not make financial sense. It also questions whether future revenues will arrive in time to cover the costs.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, let me put it in perspective, because it's not that AI itself is the problem. AI is going to be enormously productive. It's going to change how we work, how we think, how wars are fought, everything. The problem is the way it's being financed and what that does to the system.

Think of it this way. Right now, a handful of companies are spending hundreds of billions of dollars a year on data centers, on chips, on power. That spending is a very large percentage of the growth in the economy. So when you look at GDP numbers and you say, oh, the economy's strong, a big piece of that is capital expenditure on AI. And that spending is based on an expectation of future profits that haven't arrived yet. They're borrowing from the future.

That's where it starts to look like the past. I've studied the last 500 years of bubbles, and they almost all have the same features. There's a new technology that's real. Railroads were real. Radio was real. The internet was real. Then there's a lot of money flowing in, because everybody sees the technology is real and they don't want to miss it. Then the money gets funded with debt. And then prices get to a point where even if the technology works, the returns can't justify what was paid for it. In 1999, the internet changed the world exactly like people said it would, and the investors still lost eighty percent of their money.

So I look at a few things. I look at how much of the spending is being paid for with cash flow versus borrowing. I look at whether the companies are buying from each other in a circle, where one company invests in another and that company turns around and buys the first one's chips, because that makes the revenue look bigger than it really is. And I look at how concentrated it is. Most of the stock market's gains are in a very small number of companies, and most people's retirements are tied to those companies now, whether they know it or not.

Then there's the bigger picture. We have a debt problem in the United States and in most of the world. We have internal political conflict. We have a great power conflict between the United States and China, and AI is at the center of that, so it's not just an economic competition, it's a race that governments won't let anyone lose. That means there's pressure to keep spending regardless of the returns. That's when things get overdone.

So when I say it creates problems, I mean this. If it works, the productivity gains go to a relatively small number of people and companies, and that makes the wealth gap bigger, which makes the political conflict worse. And if it doesn't work on the timeline the money expects, then you have a lot of debt sitting on top of assets that can't service it, and that's how you get a financial crisis. Either way, you have to think about who wins, who loses, and what happens to the people in the middle. The technology is wonderful. It's the dynamics around it that you have to worry about.

r001.rationale: The response says companies are spending hundreds of billions based on expected future profits that have not arrived, and that the U.S.–China AI race pressures governments to keep spending regardless of returns.

astra-6.text:
Well, I’d separate the technology from the investment. A technology can change the world and still be a bad investment if you pay too much for it. When everybody believes AI is going to transform everything, that expectation gets built into prices. The question becomes: can the profits justify those prices? And who actually captures those profits?

Then there’s the broader economic issue. AI can make us much more productive, but the benefits won’t necessarily be distributed broadly. If you own the technology, you may do very well. If your work is replaced by it, you may lose income. So you can have rising productivity alongside greater inequality and greater political conflict.

That’s the tension. The capacity to produce more is a wonderful thing. But how we finance it, what we pay for it, and how we handle the consequences for people determine whether it creates prosperity or creates problems.

r001.rationale: The response discusses paying high prices for AI investments and whether profits will justify them, but does not explain that competition pressures AI developers to invest heavily despite uncertain revenue.

sol-6.1.text:
Because you have to distinguish between a technology changing the world and an investment making money. Those are two different things. AI can be enormously productive, but if everybody recognizes that and pours money into it, prices can rise to levels that the eventual profits don’t justify. You can be right about the technology and still lose money on the investment.

Then there’s the question of who captures the benefits. Does the company building the AI make the money, or does competition drive down the price so that the benefits go to the people using it? And what happens to the people whose work it replaces?

So you have this tremendous potential to create wealth, alongside a dynamic that can produce speculative excess and widen the gap between those who benefit and those who don’t. The technology itself doesn’t resolve those problems.

r001.rationale: The response says investors may pour money into AI and that competition may push prices down, but it does not explain that competition pressures AI developers to make large investments despite uncertainty about the revenue those investments will generate.
